title: The First Try
coreMove: Treat first-use resistance as implementation data and revise the checklist until the vital pause survives real workflow.
sourcePressure: The source follows an early WHO surgical-checklist pilot, initial resistance, and refinement, showing that the checklist idea becomes real only when revised into usable practice.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says people resist change and need persuasion. The real chapter says first use exposes design flaws that must be worked through.

sourceAnchors.name: early WHO surgical-checklist pilot
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar identifies the early WHO surgical-checklist pilot as the chapter's main implementation frame.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The first WHO pilot matters because the list had to be changed by the room before the room could trust it.

sourceAnchors.name: initial resistance and refinement
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar says the first try surfaces resistance and the need for refinement.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Resistance is not only a wall; sometimes it is the room telling you where the tool still does not fit.

counterintuition: Implementation matters more than the idea
tryThisNow: Ask for feedback on your checklist
examples: hospital pilot with fake outcome numbers

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Olivia, a surgical educator rehearsing a first checklist pause
exampleSpecs.audience: clinical leaders introducing a safety pause to skeptical teams
exampleSpecs.stakes: the team performs the pause once, finds it awkward, and may abandon the whole tool
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Olivia marks the exact moment the pause interrupts sterile setup and moves that item later without removing the identity and antibiotic checks
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 6:52 a.m., Olivia watches two gloved hands freeze over a blue sterile drape

exampleSpecs.domain: Etienne, a dental clinic manager testing sterilization workflow
exampleSpecs.audience: clinic managers refining a routine with assistants and dentists
exampleSpecs.stakes: a too-long checklist makes assistants skip it between patients
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Etienne times the failed first version, cuts the duplicate tray items, and keeps the sterilizer indicator check at the chair turnover point
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Etienne six ignored laminated cards to admit the first version was too slow

exampleSpecs.domain: Marta, a factory changeover pilot lead
exampleSpecs.audience: manufacturing supervisors trialing a line-start checklist
exampleSpecs.stakes: operators reject a list that asks for confirmations after the machine is already running
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Marta moves two checks to before the guard closes and deletes the items operators can see without help
exampleSpecs.firstImage: metal shavings glittering beneath the stopped press

exampleSpecs.domain: Jack, a school trip coordinator handling medication handoff
exampleSpecs.audience: teachers piloting a student safety routine outside school
exampleSpecs.stakes: a trip checklist is so long that the inhaler handoff gets lost in paperwork
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Jack rewrites the first try so the bus lead, nurse, and teacher confirm only medication owner, emergency contact, and return count before departure
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Which part of the form would actually save a child on the bus?
mustAvoid: field-trip permission slip as main object

exampleSpecs.domain: Chiara, a film set stunt safety coordinator
exampleSpecs.audience: creative crews that dislike pauses which break momentum
exampleSpecs.stakes: the first stunt checklist irritates the director and misses the actual harness risk
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Chiara listens to the stunt lead's complaint, moves the pause to before camera lock, and keeps the harness tug test visible
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "You are asking after I am already wired," the stunt lead says

exampleSpecs.domain: Yusuf, a refugee clinic intake desk lead
exampleSpecs.audience: frontline service teams adding structure without slowing urgent help
exampleSpecs.stakes: a first draft intake list delays interpreters but still misses consent for document sharing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Yusuf watches the line stall, then revises the pause to occur only when interpreter, consent, and urgent medical flag can be confirmed together
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You hear three languages in the waiting room and see the interpreter schedule slipping

skillTargets: evaluate when to cut versus keep an item

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one checklist or routine that irritates people and mark whether the irritation comes from timing, wording, length, or a missing owner.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
